'''''Helminthotheca echioides''''', known as '''bristly''' (or '''prickly''') '''oxtongue''', is a sprawling [[annual plant|annual]] or [[biennial plant|biennial]] [[herb]] native to [[Europe]] and [[North Africa]]. It was originally placed within the genus ''[[Picris]]'' but is often separated within the small genus ''[[Helminthotheca]]'' alongside a few other (mainly North African) plants which also have the distinctive outer row of bracts around the flowerheads. It is a [[Ruderal species|ruderal plant]], found on waste ground and agricultural soils around the world, and in some places it is considered a troublesome weed.

==Description==
[[File:Picris echioides in Pacifica.JPG|The seed head of ''Helminthotheca echioides''|thumb|left]]
Bristly oxtongue is an annual to biennial [[Herbaceous plant|herb]] with an erect or sprawling habit that grows up to {{convert|90|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} tall (often up to 150 cm in fertile soils and shady places),<ref name="Plantatt">{{cite web |last1=Hill |first1=M.O. |last2=Preston |first2=C.D. |last3=Roy |first3=D.B. |title=PLANTATT - Attributes of British and Irish Plants - Spreadsheet |url=https://www.brc.ac.uk/biblio/plantatt-attributes-british-and-irish-plants-spreadsheet |publisher=UK Biological Records Centre}}</ref> with a solid, furrowed stem and spreading branches. The basal rosette leaves are {{convert|10|-|20|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long, [[oblanceolate]] with a short [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]], whereas the [[cauline]] leaves are lanceolate and sessile with clasping, cordate bases. On the leaves and stem (especially on the basal leaves) there are distinctive sharp bristles, 2 mm long, with swollen whitish bases that resemble blisters. On other parts of the plant there is a scattering of smaller, anchor-shaped hairs with recurved double-pronged tips which make the plant feel sticky.<ref name=Rose>{{cite book |last1=Rose |first1=Francis |title=The Wild Flower Key |date=2006 |publisher=Frederick Warne |location=London|isbn=978-0-7232-5175-0}}</ref><ref name=Sell4>{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=P. |last2=Murrell |first2=G. |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol 4: ''Campanulaceae - Asteraceae'' |date=2006 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref>
[[File:Helminthotheca_echioides_hairs.jpg|thumb|Stiff, bulbous-based hairs on the leaf surface are characteristic of bristly oxtongue]]
[[File:Helminthotheca echioides stem.jpg|thumb|Close-up of the stem, showing typical coloration]]

In northern Europe it flowers from May to October. The [[inflorescence]]s arise on long stalks from the leaf axils in an irregular [[corymb]]. Each flowerhead is {{convert|2|-|3.5|cm|in|1|abbr=on}} wide with numerous yellow ray flowers (the outer florets sometimes tinged red/brown). They are surrounded by three rows of [[involucral bract]]s: an inner ring which is narrow and blunt-tipped with a spiny awn that arises just below the tip; a middle ring of tiny bracts which are easily overlooked and sit at the base of the inner row (they are important in separating this from other species of ''Helminthotheca'');<ref name="Holzapfel" /> and an outer ring which is made up of 3 to 5 large, ovate-cordate flaps that later surround the seed head. This outer ring of bracts are the defining feature of the genus ''[[Helminthotheca]]''.<ref>{{cite book |author1=A. R. Clapham |author2=T. G. Tutin |author3=E. F. Warburg |title=Excursion Flora of the British Isles. 3rd edition |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |isbn=0-521-23290-2 |year=1981}}</ref><ref name=Samuel1>{{cite journal |author1=Rosabelle Samuel |author2=Walter Gutermann |author3=Tod F. Stuessy |author4=Claudette F. Ruas |author5=Hans-Walter Lack |author6=Karin Tremetsberger |author7=Salvador Talavera |author8=Barbara Hermanowski |author9=Friedrich Ehrendorfer |title=Molecular phylogenetics reveals ''Leontodon'' (Asteraceae, Lactuceae) to be diphyletic |volume=93 |issue=8 |pages=1193–1205 |journal=[[American Journal of Botany]] |year=2006 |doi=10.3732/ajb.93.8.1193 |pmid=21642184|doi-access=free }}</ref>
[[File:Helminthotheca_echioides_2nd_bracts.jpg|thumb|The second ring of tiny bracts, at the base of the inner whorl, are useful in differentiating the species within the genus.]]
[[File:Helminthotheca echioides bracts.jpg|thumb|Outer and inner rows of involucral bracts on a flowerhead of bristly oxtongue]]

''Helminthotheca echioides'' is said to be heterocarpic (i.e. it has fruits of two different shapes),<ref name="Holzapfel" /> however, not all authors report this. When it is so, the outer achenes (which are  retained inside the closed-up seedhead after the central ones have dispersed) are slightly longer (7 mm) and curved, while the inner ones are only 5 mm long and straight. The normal achenes are yellow to orange or brown in colour and have transverse scaly ridges, and a narrowed tip (beak) about as long as the body, to which is affixed a pappus of two rows of white, feathery plumes which enable the seeds to be dispersed by the wind. Reproduction is believed to be [[apomixis|apomictic]], so the plants effectively clone themselves, but the flowers are also visited by bees.<ref name="Sell4" />
[[File:Helminthotheca echioides sl17.jpg|thumb|The seeds of bristly oxtongue apparently resemble the eggs of intestinal parasites.]]
[[File:Helminthotheca echioides heterocarpic.jpg|thumb|The outermost fruits in a flowerhead are sometimes different to the ones on the disk.]]

==Taxonomy==
The genus ''Helminthotheca'' was originally described by the pre-Linnean author [[Sébastien Vaillant]] in 1754 but, because such names are ruled out by the [[International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants|Code of Nomenclature]], the recognised author is [[Johann Gottfried Zinn]], who listed it in his ''Description of the flora around Göttingen'' in 1757. However, [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] had by this time already published a valid name for bristly oxtongue in ''[[Species Plantarum]]'', so Linnaeus's name, ''Picris echioides'', is the [[basionym]] and has precedence over the name Zinn used. Prickly oxtongue has therefore been assigned to two different genera from earliest days, but the combination of Zinn's ''Helminthotheca'' and Linnaeus's ''echioides'' was not formed until 1973, when the name was coined by the Czech botanist [[Josef Ludwig Holub|Josef Holub]] in a paper in the journal ''[https://www.jstor.org/journal/foligeobphyt Folia Geobotanica & Phytotaxonomica]''. In the English-speaking world, endorsement for the new combination was given by Walter Lack in a paper in the journal [[Taxon (journal)|''Taxon'']] in 1975.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Global Biodiversity Information Facility |title=Helminthotheca Zinn |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/100349958/verbatim}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=International Plant Names index |title=Helminthotheca Zinn |url=https://www.ipni.org/n/9275-1 |access-date=21 September 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lack |first1=H.W. |title=Type specimens of the Linnaean species of Picris L. (Compositae) |journal=Taxon |date=1975 |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=113–116|doi=10.2307/1219007 |jstor=1219007 }}</ref>

Many other synonyms for ''Helminthotheca echioides'' have been coined over the years, which are listed in the  [https://www.gbif.org/species/100350115 International Cichorieae Network: Cichorieae Portal].

Modern molecular studies show that ''Picris'' and ''Helminthotheca'' are closely related. The studies are consistent with the current view that they be considered separate genera. Anatomically, they are separated mainly by the presence of an outer row of enlarged involucral bracts in ''Helminthotheca''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Samuel |first1=R. |last2=Stuessy |first2=S.T. |last3=Tremetsberger |first3=K. |title=Phylogenetic relationships among species of ''Hypochaeris'' (Asteraceae, Cichorieae) based on its plastid TRNL intron, TRNL-F spacer, and MATK sequences |journal=American Journal of Botany |date=2003 |volume=90 |issue=3 |pages=496–507 |doi=10.3732/ajb.90.3.496|pmid=21659142 }}</ref><ref name="Samuel1" />

Its chromosome number is 2''n'' = 10.<ref name="CABI" />

''Helminthotheca echioides'' is not known to hybridise with any other species.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=Hybridization and the Flora of the British Isles |date=1975 |publisher=Academic Press |location=London |isbn=0-12-661650-7}}</ref>

A number of [[infraspecific taxon|infraspecific taxa]] have been described, varying in their leaf shape,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bsbi.org.uk/HuntsNov08.pdf |title=Huntingdonshire Newsletter |year=2008 |author=David Broughton |publisher=[[Botanical Society of the British Isles]]}}</ref> although they are not widely accepted. Sell & Murrell<ref name="Sell4" /> list four varieties in Britain:

* var. mollis <small>(Duby) P.D. Sell</small>, with large dentate but not incised leaves

* var. pratensis <small>(Chevall.) P.D. Sell</small>, narrowly elliptical dentate leaves

* var. echioides, with broadly elliptical leaves

* var. incisa <small>P.D. Sell</small>, with large, deeply incised leaves.

The generic name ''Helminthotheca'' derives from the Ancient Greek {{Lang|grc|ἕλμινθος}} (helmins, helminthos), which means "intestinal worm", and θήκη (theca), which is a box or a case (used in anatomy and zoology to describe the sheath around an organ), to make the word "worm-case". It refers to the appearance of the seeds of oxtongue, which look rather like nematode eggs.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Wiktionary |title=Helminth |date=6 February 2023 |url=https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/helminth}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Jepson Herbarium |title=Helminthotheca |url=https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=81751}}</ref> The "theca" part of the name might be a reference to the way the capitulum closes up after fruiting, trapping some of the seeds within the "case" of the dead flowerhead.<ref name=Grieve>{{cite book |last1=Grieve |first1=Maud |title=A Modern Herbal |date=1931 |publisher=Dover Publications Inc. |location=New York |isbn=0-486-22798-7}}</ref><ref name=Holzapfel>{{cite journal |last1=Holzapfel |first1=S. |title=A revision of the genus Picris (Asteraceae, Lactuceae) s.l. in Australia |journal=Willdenowia |date=1994 |volume=21 |issue=1/2 |pages=97–218 |jstor=3996683 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3996683}}</ref> The [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] ''echioides'' comes from the similarity of the [[leaf|leaves]] to those of [[Echium vulgare|viper's bugloss]], which also have blister-like hairs on the surface.<ref>{{cite book |author=H. Genaust |year=2005 |title=Etymologisches Wörterbuch der botanischen Pflanzennamen |language=German |isbn=3-937872-16-7 |publisher=[[Nikol-Verlag]]}}</ref>
The suffix ''{{linktext|-oides}}'' means "-like".<ref>{{cite book|last1=Wright|first1=Charles Henry|last2=Dewar|first2=Daniel|title=Johnson's Gardener's Dictionary|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RL1HAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA1066|year=1894|publisher=G. Bell|page=1066|quote= -oides, -like}}</ref>

The common name also describes the shape and appearance of the leaves.

==Similar species==
[[Picris hieracioides|Hawkweed oxtongue]] has very similar flowers to bristly oxtongue, but they can easily be separate by these features:
* Hawkweed oxtongue: no blisters on the leaves, distinctly wavy edges to the leaves, and recurved bracts around the flowerheads
* Bristly oxtongue: blisters on the leaves and the characteristic bracts around the flowerhead.

At the rosette stage, there are two plants in Britain which are very similar to bristly oxtongue: [[Echium vulgare|viper's bugloss]] and [[Dipsacus fullonum|teasel]].
* Viper's bugloss has distinctly more dense rosettes, more glaucous leaves with a concolorous central vein (reddish or pale in bristly oxtongue) and is covered in long (3 mm) hairs.
* Teasel has large spines along the midrib on the lower side of the leaves.<ref name="Rose" /><ref name=Poland>{{cite book |last1=Poland |first1=John |last2=Clement |first2=Eric |title=The Vegetative Key to the British Flora |date=2009 |publisher=John Poland |location=Southampton |isbn=978-0-9560144-0-5}}</ref>

==Distribution and status==
[[File:Helminthotheca echioides rays.jpg|thumb|Outer rays of bristly oxtongue are sometimes red striped.]]
''Helminthotheca echioides'' is thought to be native to [[North Africa]] and the [[Mediterranean Basin]], where it grows in semi-arid conditions that are reproduced in the [[ruderal]] habitats associated with agriculture and the disturbed soils created by human activity throughout the world. As a result, it has spread as a [[weed]] to all the continents (except mainland Antarctica), and it is often abundant in farmland and towns.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Global Biodiversity Information Facility |title=Helminthotheca echioides (L) Holub |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/3141855}}</ref>

The IUCN has not yet assessed the global status of bristly oxtongue,<ref>{{Cite web |title=The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species |url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250129173819/https://www.iucnredlist.org/ |archive-date=2025-01-29 |access-date=2025-01-31 |website=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species |url-status=live }}</ref> but where it has been assessed within its native range, it is generally assigned to the category LC ([[Least-concern species|least concern]]).<ref>{{Cite web |title=PlantAtlas |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.6y7gxt |access-date=2025-01-31 |website=plantatlas2020.org}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Cheffings |first1=C.M. | last2=Farrell |first2=L. |title=The Vascular Plant Red Data List for Great Britain |date=2005 |publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee |location=Peterborough}}</ref>
<ref>{{Cite web |title=Picride fausse vipérine, Helminthothèque fausse vipérine, Picris fausse vipérine |url=https://inpn.mnhn.fr/espece/cd_nom/101210/tab/statut |access-date=31 January 2024 |website=Inventaire National du Patrimoine Natural}}</ref>

In [[Great Britain]] it is common in the south and east and more patchily distributed to the north and west, whereas it is rare in [[Ireland]]. It is considered to be an [[archaeophyte]] (ancient introduction) throughout the [[British Isles]], and it is thought to be increasing in many areas.<ref name=Lockton>{{cite book |last1=Lockton |first1=Alex |last2=Whild |first2=Sarah |title=The Flora and Vegetation of Shropshire |date=2015 |publisher=Shropshire Botanical Society |location=Montford Bridge |url=https://archive.org/details/flora-and-vegetation-of-shropshire-2015|isbn=978-0-9530937-2-4}}</ref><ref name=Atlas>{{cite book |title=New Atlas of the British and Irish Flora |author1=C.D. Preston |author2=D.A. Pearman |author3=T.D. Dines |year=2002 |isbn=0-19-851067-5 |pages=928 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]}}</ref>

It has been introduced to [[North America]], where it can now be found from [[Nova Scotia]] to [[British Columbia]] and [[California]], and it is classified as an invasive weed.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Helminthotheca echioides - FNA |url=http://floranorthamerica.org/Helminthotheca_echioides |access-date=2025-01-31 |website=floranorthamerica.org}}</ref>

It was first noticed in Australia in 1871 and has since spread to most parts of the country.<ref name="Holzapfel" />

==Ecology==
[[File:Helminthotheca echioides habitat.jpg|thumb|Typical habitat for bristly oxtongue, along a verge]]
[[File:Helminthotheca echioides pavement.jpg|thumb|Bristly oxtongue growing as a pavement weed]]
Bristly oxtongue is an opportunist species which will colonise [[disturbed ground]] very quickly. It is considered to act as a [[Raunkiær plant life-form#Therophytes|therophyte]], which completes its life cycle quickly, or a [[Raunkiær plant life-form#Hemicryptophytes|hemicryptophyte]], which has a basal rosette to survive unfavourable conditions such as winter or drought. The feathery pappus allows seeds to be widely dispersed by the wind, but it has no capacity for vegetative spread (for example, by stolons or bulbs).<ref name="Plantatt" />  Typical habitats for it include waste ground, field margins, sea walls, road verges and banks on clay soils or chalk.<ref name="Atlas" /> One reason for its success is that it is particularly resistant to drought, being able to sprout from basal shoots after dry periods.<ref name=CABI>{{cite web |last1=CABI |title=Invasive Species Compendium: Helminthotheca echioides datasheet |url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/116335#C0E835BF-79D3-470E-9081-BC5C53927CD3 |access-date=30 September 2022}}</ref>

It generally grows in places where there is full sunlight, whilst also tolerating partial shade, for example, by hedgerows; it requires moderately damp soils with a slightly alkaline reaction; and it prefers moderately fertile conditions. The [[Indicator value|Ellenberg values]] in Britain are L = 7, F = 5, R = 7, N = 6, and S = 0.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hill|first1=M.O.|last2=Mountford|first2=J.O.|last3=Roy|first3=D.B.|last4=Bunce|first4=R.G.H.|title=Ellenberg's indicator values for British plants. ECOFACT Volume 2. Technical Annex|date=1999|publisher=Institute of Terrestrial Ecology|isbn=1870393481|url=http://nora.nerc.ac.uk/6411/1/ECOFACT2a.pdf|accessdate=29 May 2017}}</ref>

It is a lowland plant in the [[British Isles]], recorded only up to 370 m (in south [[Wales]]).<ref>{{cite web |last1=Pearman |first1=D.A. |title=Altitudinal Limits of British Plants, 2021 |url=https://bsbi.org/altitudes}}</ref>

The UK [http://dbif.brc.ac.uk/ Database of Insects and their Food Plants] lists four species that make use of bristly oxtongue. The larvae of the [[fly]] ''[[Tephritis separata]]'', which is widespread throughout Europe and Asia, live on the flowers. The [[Hymenoptera|wasp]] ''Phanacis caulicola'' <small>(Hedicke, 1939)</small> has larvae that tunnel chambers inside the stem, leaving no visible sign of their presence until they emerge.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Dorset Nature |title=Galls - Phanacis caulicola |url=https://www.dorsetnature.co.uk/pages-gall/g-257.html |access-date=22 September 2022}}</ref> Two moths also live on this species: ''[[Cochylis hybridella|Neocochylis hybridella]]'' caterpillars feed within the seedheads,<ref>{{cite web |last1=UK Moths |title=49.136 BF965 Neocochylis hybridella |url=https://www.ukmoths.org.uk/species/neocochylis-hybridella/ |access-date=22 September 2022}}</ref> and the [[tortrix]] moth ''[[Aethes tesserana]]'' larvae feed within the roots.<ref>{{cite web |last1=UK Moths |title=49.121 BF939 Aethes tesserana |url=https://www.ukmoths.org.uk/species/aethes-tesserana/ |access-date=22 September 2022}}</ref> Both these species are also widespread in Europe and western Asia.

==Uses==
The leaves were formerly used as a pot herb, and were "esteemed good to relax the bowels".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bryant |first1=Charles |title=Flora Diaetetica, or History of Esculent Plants |date=1783 |publisher=B. White |location=London |page=141 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6XjuiSEZ6fwC&pg=PR1}}</ref> There are also various reports of it being used as an [[antihelmintic|antihelminthic]] treatment, although this may be due to confusion about the meaning of its name.<ref>{{cite book |author1=M. A. Fischer |author2=W. Adler |author3=K. Oswald |title=Exkursionsflora für Österreich, Liechtenstein und Südtirol. 2nd ed. |language=German |publisher=Biologiezentrum der Oberösterreichischen Landesmuseen |year=2005}}</ref><ref name="Grieve" /> The English herbalist [[Nicholas Culpeper]] considered "lang de boeuf" to be a good cure for melancholy (when steeped in wine), and a general alexipharmic (antidote to unspecified toxins).<ref>{{cite book |last1=Potterton |first1=David |title=Culpeper's Colour Herbal |date=2002 |isbn=978-0572027940}}</ref>

Although it is not a popular culinary herb, some foragers like to use the flowers to flavour vinegar.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Julia's Edible Weeds |title=Bristly Oxtongue |date=25 April 2022 |url=https://www.juliasedibleweeds.com/general/bristly-oxtongue/ |access-date=24 September 2022}}</ref>

Some pet owners feed bristly oxtongue to their [[Tortoise|tortoises]], but they do not like it.<ref>{{cite web |last1=The Tortoise Table |title=Bristly Oxtongue |url=https://www.thetortoisetable.org.uk/plant-database/viewplants/?plant=64&c=6#.Yy7iYnbMK3A |access-date=24 September 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=King |first1=Linda |title=Edible Plants for Tortoises in the UK |date=2020 |publisher=Linkingarts |isbn=9780993417634 |edition=4}}</ref>
